open_obligations: Check that high-confidence errors in Khan et al.'s data are rare enough to address Bowman et al.'s high-stakes concern.
Note the different protocol: two opposing debaters versus one dialog assistant.
Check calibration curves in the high-confidence regime, where Michael et al. report difficulty.
in.other_title: Confident human debate judgements are reliable: 94% accuracy keeping 65% of questions
in.rationale: Bowman et al. report participants sometimes give confidently wrong judgements and accept confident false model claims in human-model chat. Khan et al. report that rejecting human debate judgements below 75% confidence keeps 65% of questions at 94% accuracy, that debate beats consultancy at all rejection thresholds, and that judges are better calibrated with debate; the protocol and task differ (LLM debate on QuALITY HARD vs chat on MMLU and QuALITY).
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether high-confidence human judgements are reliable when judges are assisted by debate rather than a single model, on QuALITY HARD

open_obligations: Check the share of confidently wrong answers under debate, not only the Brier score.
Note the domain differs (contested health claims vs MMLU and QuALITY).
Check whether overconfidence differs by prior-belief group.
in.other_title: Human judges are overconfident under both protocols; debate Brier 0.231 vs 0.335
in.rationale: Bowman et al. report participants sometimes give highly confident wrong judgements. Rahman et al. report judges are overconfident under both debate and consultancy, most above 80% confidence, but debate gives better calibration (Brier 0.231 vs 0.335); the setting is binary factuality claims with GPT-4o agents.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether human judges assisted by AI are overconfident, for debate versus consultancy on COVID-19 claims

text: The authors state their results are not strong enough to validate the human-model chat protocol for high-stakes use, because participants sometimes give highly confident judgments that are wrong and sometimes accept false but confident, plausible-sounding claims from the model, given their limited domain knowledge and ability to fact-check.
title: Participants sometimes accept confident false model claims with high confidence
